analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to safeguard personal data, notify people of breaches, and lets consumers freeze their credit reports.
analysis.headline: The Identity Theft Protection Act won bipartisan committee approval in December 2005 but was never brought to a Senate vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a string of huge data breaches, this bill would have required any company holding sensitive personal data to run a written security program, tell consumers when a breach puts them at risk of identity theft, and let consumers freeze their credit reports so thieves cannot open accounts in their names. It would also restrict the use and sale of Social Security numbers. The version the Senate Commerce Committee reported, however, would have wiped out stronger state breach-notification and security-freeze laws, barred consumers from suing violators, and let credit bureaus charge fees for freezes. The Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose data companies hold. They would gain a federal right to be told when a breach exposes them to identity theft, the power to freeze their credit reports, free freezes for identity-theft victims, and new limits on how companies collect, display, and sell Social Security numbers.

how_it_helps.text: Any company or nonprofit that keeps sensitive personal information would have to maintain a written security program with administrative, technical, and physical safeguards [S3][S4].
A company that discovers a breach creating a reasonable risk of identity theft would have to notify each affected person, generally within 45 days of discovery [S3][S4].

Consumers could place a security freeze on their credit report, blocking the bureaus from releasing it to third parties without authorization, and identity-theft victims could get freezes free of charge [S3][S4].

The bill would restrict unnecessary collection of Social Security numbers, bar printing them on ID cards and driver's licenses, and generally ban selling Social Security numbers or displaying them publicly [S3][S4].
State attorneys general could sue violators on behalf of their residents, and the FTC could seek civil penalties of up to $11,000 per affected individual [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect and sell consumer data — retailers, banks, data brokers, credit bureaus, universities, and others — would bear the cost of security programs, breach investigations, notifications, and freeze administration; the FTC gets $1 million a year to enforce it.

drawbacks.text: The reported bill preempts state security-program, breach-notification, and security-freeze laws [S4], so consumers in states with stronger rules — such as states requiring notice for every breach — would lose those protections in exchange for the weaker federal floor.

It expressly bars any private right of action or class action under the Act, and restricts state-law suits to attorneys general [S4], so a consumer whose identity was stolen after a company's security failure could not recover damages directly.

Individual notification is required only when the company itself determines the breach creates a 'reasonable risk of identity theft' — the company makes that judgment — and breaches under 1,000 people with no such risk need only be reported quietly to the FTC [S3][S4].

Companies can use cheaper 'substitute notice' (email, website posting, media) when direct notice costs over $250,000 or covers more than 500,000 people, and the FTC is barred from mandating any specific security technology [S4].

Cable, telecom, and internet carriers are exempt from the breach and safeguard rules for communications they transmit, and financial firms are deemed in compliance if they follow existing Gramm-Leach-Bliley rules, enforced by their own banking regulators [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the core gains are real: a federal breach-notice right, credit freezes, and Social Security number protections. But the committee substitute traded away a lot to get industry on board — it would override tougher state laws, eliminate consumers' ability to sue, let companies decide when a breach is serious enough to warrant notice, and cap penalties. A person living in a state with strong breach-notification laws could actually end up with weaker protection under this bill than under the status quo.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved it and it sat on the Senate's calendar of business for over a year, but Senate leadership never brought it to the floor, and it died when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Gordon Smith introduced the bill on July 14, 2005, joined by six colleagues including Democrats Bill Nelson, Daniel Inouye, Mark Pryor, and Hillary Clinton and Republicans Ted Stevens and John McCain [S4][S5].
The Commerce Committee ordered it reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute in July 2005, and it was formally reported on December 8, 2005, with a written report [S6].

The committee substitute softened the original bill: it added broad preemption of state security, breach-notification, and freeze laws, a ban on technology mandates, an exemption for telecom and cable carriers, and deemed-compliance for firms following Gramm-Leach-Bliley rules [S3][S4].
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 320) on December 8, 2005, and no further action was ever taken [S4][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies holding consumer data are better off: no federal security or breach-notification mandate was enacted, and consumers kept whatever protections their state laws already provided — including stronger state freeze and notification laws, since the bill's preemption never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers, credit bureaus, and data-holding companies

for.name: Sen. Gordon Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through introduction and committee consideration.

for.name: Sen. Ted Stevens
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and, as chairman, reported it out of committee with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on December 8, 2005.

for.name: Six Senate cosponsors (4 Democrats, 2 Republicans at introduction)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction: Bill Nelson (FL), Daniel Inouye (HI), Mark Pryor (AR), Hillary Clinton (NY), Ted Stevens (AK), and John McCain (AZ), giving it bipartisan backing; seven cosponsors in total [S5].

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote; it sat on the legislative calendar from December 2005 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Financial services and data broker industries
against.role: Industries holding and selling consumer data
against.what_they_did: Lobbied for a single federal standard overriding stricter state breach and freeze laws, and for protection from consumer lawsuits; the committee substitute's preemption and no-private-action provisions track those asks.

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote ever occurred, but the bill itself was bipartisan: a Republican sponsor with seven cosponsors split 4 Democrats and 3 Republicans, and a Republican chairman reported it favorably with Democratic support [S5][S6].

industries.industry: Credit bureaus and consumer reporting agencies
industries.note: Freeze rights would limit their ability to sell credit reports, but they could charge fees for freezes (free only for documented ID-theft victims), and the bill preempts stricter state freeze laws. Reseller agencies and check- and deposit-account reporting firms are exempted entirely [S4].

industries.industry: Companies holding consumer data (retailers, data brokers, universities, nonprofits)
industries.note: They would face new security-program, breach-investigation, and notification duties, but gain preemption of tougher state laws, no private lawsuits, penalty caps, the ability to decide when a breach merits individual notice, and quiet FTC-only reporting for small breaches [S3][S4].

Firms complying with existing Gramm-Leach-Bliley rules are deemed compliant with the bill's safeguards and notification requirements, and enforcement shifts to their own prudential regulators and state insurance authorities rather than the FTC [S4].

industries.industry: Telecom, cable, and internet service providers
industries.note: They are exempted from the safeguard and breach-notification requirements for third-party communications stored in their networks during transmission [S4].
